# {{< var workshop.name >}} {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.home-lead}
The course takes published claims, the reanalyses that each of them received in a many-analyst study and the replications that tested them with new data, and teaches reproduction, robustness and replication in R, from the data and code of real studies. One exercise runs through every case study, and each case study has a site of its own.
:::

## Case studies {#the-cases .unnumbered .home-reveal}

::: {.home-intro .home-reveal}
The case studies differ in the statistics and the data handling that they ask for, from a comparison of proportions in one public file of emails to a panel of country-years built from sixteen licensed surveys, and each site offers the formats that its case study allows, with slide decks of its own and a companion of the methods that the case study can teach. Further case studies are in preparation.
:::

:::: {.home-cases}

::: {.home-casecard .home-reveal}
[1]{.home-rung}

### [Housing and racial bias](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-housing/) {#housing-and-racial-bias .unnumbered .unlisted}

In a field experiment published in the *American Journal of Political Science* in 2017, the same short email was sent to about a thousand public housing authorities in the United States, each time signed with one of six names meant to indicate a white, a Black or a Hispanic sender. The claim, in the form in which the robustness study of SCORE [Multi100\; @AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness] gave it to its analysts, is that "Hispanic housing applicants were ... less likely to be greeted by name than were ... white counterparts" [@EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect, abstract].

<details class="home-more">
<summary>More about the case study</summary>

**What it teaches.** Proportions and the chi-square test, the linear probability model set against the logit, what conditioning on a reply does to an experiment, randomisation inference and statistical power.

**The data.** One file of 1,014 emails, released into the public domain (CC0) and shipped with the workspace.

::: {.home-3r}
- **Reproduction.** SCORE never attempted one, although the data and code are public. The four statistics recorded for the analysts in the robustness study reproduce exactly from the public file.
- **Robustness.** Three of the five analysts of the robustness study found evidence for the claim, and the other two found evidence neither way.
- **Replication.** A new preregistered experiment, emailing 3,050 housing authorities under new names, found no significant gap (z = 0.66, p = 0.51).
:::

</details>

[Go to the site of the case study](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-housing/){.home-go}
:::

::: {.home-casecard .home-reveal}
[2]{.home-rung}

### [Europeanisation and the economy](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-eu/) {#europeanisation-and-the-economy .unnumbered .unlisted}

An article published in the *European Sociological Review* in 2016 drew on Eurobarometer surveys conducted between 2004 and 2013 to examine whether the economic crisis had changed the meanings that citizens attach to the European Union. The claim, in the form in which the robustness study gave it to its analysts, is that "... poor economic performances ... decrease positive dimensions of EU framing" [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic, p. 619].

<details class="home-more">
<summary>More about the case study</summary>

**What it teaches.** Aggregating repeated cross-sections into a panel, fixed and random effects and the within–between model, inference with few clusters, and a multiverse of 864 specifications.

**The data.** A panel of 270 country-years built from Eurobarometer surveys and shipped with the workspace. The respondent files behind it come from the GESIS archive, under a free account and terms that do not allow them to be passed on.

::: {.home-3r}
- **Reproduction.** Two attempts to reproduce the published result from the original materials did not succeed.
- **Robustness.** All five analysts of the robustness study concluded that the data support the claim, while the partial correlations recorded for their results run from −0.006 to −0.452.
- **Replication.** A replication on later Eurobarometer waves was judged not successful.
:::

</details>

[Go to the site of the case study](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-eu/){.home-go}
:::

## Formats {.unnumbered .home-reveal}

::: {.home-intro .home-reveal}
The course is taught in three formats, and the facilitator of each course chooses its format and its case study. Each format is an ordered route through the pages of the site of its case study, with a sidebar of its own and the slide deck that it uses, so that the link that you receive for a course leads straight to its route.
:::

:::: {.home-grid}

::: {.home-track .home-reveal}
### Short {.unnumbered .unlisted}

[Two halves, in the browser]{.home-meta}

One case study with nothing to install and nothing preregistered, worked on the slides themselves, which run R inside the browser: the claim and the five reanalyses, the estimand statement, the reproduction of one reanalysis of your choice, the menu of analyses and the curve of the claim, and the replication with new data.

[Housing](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-housing/tracks/short/), [Europeanisation](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-eu/tracks/short/).
:::

::: {.home-track .home-reveal}
### Day {.unnumbered .unlisted}

[Four parts, in your IDE]{.home-meta}

One case study in four parts, worked in the downloadable workspace in your IDE, while the slides, which run R inside the browser, show each step with its output and stand in for the workspace if an installation fails: the claim and the credibility of social science, the estimand and the causal graph, the reproduction of one reanalysis chosen by each participant, and robustness, with the menu of defensible analyses, the class chart, the curve of the claim and one analysis declared before it runs.

[Housing](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-housing/tracks/day/), [Europeanisation](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-eu/tracks/day/).
:::

::: {.home-track .home-reveal}
### Independent {.unnumbered .unlisted}

[At your own pace, in R]{.home-meta}

The site of each case study holds a route for a reader who works alone, which takes the case study through the five tasks with the modules of its companion between them and ends on a project of your own.

[Housing](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-housing/tracks/independent/), [Europeanisation](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-eu/tracks/independent/).
:::

## Methods and tools {.unnumbered .home-reveal}

::: {.home-intro .home-reveal}
The companion of each site holds the methods that arise from its case study, from what its original authors or its five analysts did or from the shape of its data. The estimand and the causal graph, the multiverse and the common scale of the five analysts are taught on every site, because every exercise rests on them. The tools serve every case study and are taught once, on this site, with the file of the Housing case study as their running example: the installation and the setup help, and the modules on R, the IDE, Quarto, and Git and GitHub, all in the Tools menu. The table maps each case study onto its formats and onto these modules and those of its companion, and each name in the table links to the module that teaches it.
:::

## SCORE {.unnumbered .home-reveal}

::: {.home-intro .home-reveal}
The claims of the case studies come from the work of SCORE, short for Systematizing Confidence in Open Research and Evidence, a programme that put claims from published social and behavioural research through three kinds of repetition [@AlipourfardEtAl2021SystematizingConfidenceOpen]. A reproduction repeats the original analysis on the original data, a robustness check applies different but defensible analyses to the same data, and a replication asks the same question of new data. In the robustness study, 457 analysts produced 504 reanalyses of 100 claims, at least five for each, from the data of the original studies [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness, p. 136], and the exercise of the course follows its design on a smaller scale.
:::

:::: {.home-cases .home-reveal}

::: {.home-r}
### [SCORE](score.qmd) {.unnumbered .unlisted}

The programme and its three studies, how the robustness study chose its claims and set its two tasks, and what the record holds for each case study.
:::

::: {.home-r}
### [The robustness article](robustness-article.qmd) {#the-robustness-article .unnumbered .unlisted}

How the robustness study placed 504 reanalyses on one scale, what that scale assumes, what the article found, and what to ask of an effect size converted for comparison.
:::

## Getting started {.unnumbered .home-reveal}

::: {.home-intro .home-reveal}
The short format needs only a browser, because its tasks are done on the slides, which run R inside the browser. The day and independent formats are worked in the workspace of the case study, with R, Quarto and an IDE installed beforehand.
:::

:::: {.home-steps .home-reveal}

::: {.home-step}
### R and an IDE {.unnumbered .unlisted}

Install R, Quarto and an IDE (Positron, RStudio, VS Code, etc.), following the steps for your operating system. [Install and check](setup.qmd)
:::

::: {.home-step}
### The workspace {.unnumbered .unlisted}

Download the workspace from the site of your case study, open it in your IDE and run the check script. [Housing](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-housing/tracks/day/before.html#the-workspace), [Europeanisation](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-eu/tracks/day/before.html#the-workspace)
:::

::: {.home-step}
### Setup help {.unnumbered .unlisted}

The checks to run first, the problems that participants have met, and what to ask an AI assistant or a person when something fails. [Setup help](help.qmd)
:::

::: {.home-step}
### Git and GitHub {.unnumbered .unlisted}

Putting your own reanalysis under version control and publishing the rendered report, once the course is over. [Git and GitHub](git-github.qmd)
:::

## Chris Moreh {.unnumbered}

::: {.home-role}
Lecturer in Sociology, Newcastle University
:::

<!-- The biography is quoted from chrismoreh.com (source: D:/GitHub/chrismoreh-source/index.qmd), as CM asked on 2026-10-25, and copied verbatim from the opening page of the Europeanisation site. -->

A social scientist interested in the political sociology of migration, mobility, ethnicity and nationalism.

Hailing from Transylvania, trained in anthropology and sociology at [Eötvös Loránd University of Budapest](https://tatk.elte.hu/en/) and [Central European University](https://sociology.ceu.edu/), and with a PhD from [Northumbria University](https://www.northumbria.ac.uk/), I currently work as a Lecturer (Assistant Professor) in Sociology at [Newcastle University (UK)](https://www.ncl.ac.uk/gps/staff/profile/chrismoreh.html).

I approach social research as a comparative, interdisciplinary and multimethodological endeavour. My work has combined ethnographic observation, document analysis, survey methods and statistical modelling.

I'm enthusiastic about transparency and reproducibility in the social sciences, and my [pedagogical approach](https://www.ncl.ac.uk/mediav8/library/file-downloads/research-services/open-research/moreh.pdf) seeks to develop skills that facilitate open and credible research practices.

[chrismoreh.com](https://chrismoreh.com)
